what: ROCK DOMAIN PACK (evidence rank 4, G3) for case rock1: what the rock most likely is, grain, mineral colours, fracture style, edge rounding, and loose-rock 3-D proportions for the UNSEEN back. Written 2026-10-18 by the rock-pack agent. Every value carries source + confidence (G2) and a status label: checked (a proven tool measured it), estimated (sourced or reasoned, not measured), unchecked.
status: ESTIMATED overall. Photo measurements are in cases/rock1/pack_evidence/grain_probe.json (tool grain_probe.py; its self-test on planted textures passes on both sides; the held-out downscale test only PARTLY passes, see grain.photo_measured). Nothing here is a 3-D reference; the back stays LABELLED estimated (R6).
units: mm unless stated; px = ref.jpg pixels (1728x1152); colours sRGB 0-255 as SEEN (lit, apparent), not albedo
confidence_scale: high = measured on the photo with a proven tool, or a stable textbook definition; medium = cited source on this rock family, or a photo read by eye that several cues agree on; low = weak/vendor source, or a cited source on a different rock/setting; estimate = no source, reasoning only, flagged

scale_link.value: 0.70 m largest horizontal extent (the person's decision, NOTES.md 2026-10-18) over a measured silhouette width of 1047 px -> 0.669 mm/px at the rock (ignores perspective: near and far parts differ by a few %)
scale_link.status: estimated (silhouette by threshold L<205; the builder's R1 mask supersedes it)
scale_link.caveat: The real rock's size is unknown. Grain sizes are given two ways: (a) as photographed at the chosen 0.70 m scale, which is what the model must reproduce (R4); (b) the typical natural range for the rock type. A 0.70 m rock of this type would show grains of about 2-6 mm, and the photo at 0.70 m scale shows about 2.5-7 mm, so the chosen scale is plausible.

what_i_see: Uniformly speckled, medium grey overall, no layering across the whole body (photo, by eye)

Grains: black/dark grey (about 1/3 of area), white to pale grey (about 1/3), mid grey, and a minority of beige/buff grains; no pink or salmon grains (photo, by eye; k-means in pack_evidence/grain_probe.json gives 5 near-neutral clusters, all with a slight warm cast R-B = 6-8)
Equigranular-looking texture with no large phenocrysts (photo)
Angular, blocky body of near-planar faces meeting at sub-angular edges, with re-entrant notches where blocks step back (photo)
Faint parallel linear streaks on the upper right face (about x 1050-1150, y 200-350): a weak foliation, or fracture-surface ribs (photo, uncertain)

best_reading.value: grey quartz-poor to intermediate plutonic rock: diorite / quartz diorite / granodiorite (salt-and-pepper grey granitoid)
best_reading.why: White + black speckle with near-neutral grey overall and no pink K-feldspar fits diorite/granodiorite (white plagioclase + black hornblende/biotite). Granite is usually lighter and often pinkish from K-feldspar. Quartz content, the real separator, cannot be judged from a photo.

sources.says: diorite: white to pale grey plagioclase + dark green to black hornblende give the salt-and-pepper look; <5 % visible quartz vs >20 % in granite/granodiorite
granodiorite described as fine to medium grained and medium grey on fresh and weathered surfaces (one mapped body)
a granodiorite grey on fresh surfaces, brownish-reddish stain where weathered

alternatives.why: same speckle; would usually show more clear quartz and some pinkish feldspar, none seen
only cue is the faint streaking on one face; gneiss shows light/dark bands and aligned micas, which the rest of the body does not

source.says: gneiss = distinct banding, parallel or wavy; uniformly speckled rock is more likely granite; small specimens may not show banding

identification.consequence_for_build: All readings share the build-relevant traits: coarse granular speckle, blocky jointed fracture, granular rough faces. Default grain is ISOTROPIC (estimate); only if the lineation is confirmed (gneiss) add a weak directional anisotropy near the upper right face.

source.says: fine <1 mm, medium 1-5 mm (sugar to pea), coarse 5 mm-3 cm, very coarse >3 cm

sources.says: granodiorite mostly fine to medium grained
biotite blocky grains up to ~3 mm, hornblende up to ~2 mm in an Australian granodiorite sample (search summary)
a granodiorite with roughly isometric grains 2-6 mm (search summary; not read in full)

visible_grain_diameter_mm_at_0.70m.how: grain diameter ~2-3 x the autocorrelation 1/e radius for a two-phase speckle, cross-read by eye (grains about 4-10 px)

photo_measured.proof: A22 planted textures of known blob size: x0.5 -> measured x0.53, x2 -> x2.04 (both sides pass). A23 held-out: the photo downscaled x0.5 on crops fixed before the run gives ratios 0.58-0.68, NOT 0.5: at about 2 px the photo's grain sits near the pixel/JPEG resolution floor, so its finest grains are unresolved and the measured length is biased up by about 15-35 %.
photo_measured.status: estimated (tool proven on planted data; on the photo it is resolution-limited, so read it as an upper bound at the fine end)
photo_measured.build_rule: R4 compares the grain spectrum of render vs photo at the PHOTO's resolution: judge the texture through the same camera and pixel size, not by these mm values alone

relief_mm.source: estimate: granular fracture surfaces are rough at about grain scale (feldspar breaks on flat cleavage steps, quartz conchoidally), so relief ~0.1-0.4 grain diameter; the photo shows grains as colour spots with fine sparkle, not as deep pits

related_source.says: granular fracture = surfaces produced by aggregated minerals, e.g. granite; uneven fracture = rough by minute elevations and depressions

relief_mm.build_rule: Grain is mineral COLOUR plus this small relief (R4: never relief painted as colour)

mineral_colours.note: Apparent sRGB under the studio light, from k-means (k=5) on four interior 128 px crops of the big faces (grain_probe.json). Clusters mix minerals with shading; the mapping to minerals is by eye + source.

clusters_apparent.mineral: mafic grains in light + shaded feldspar

beige_grains.value: a minority (by eye about 5 % of area) of buff/beige grains, approx sRGB (175,160,135)
beige_grains.source: photo by eye; weathering stain per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pi%C3%A9gut-Pluviers_Granodiorite
beige_grains.confidence: low; k-means at k=5 did not separate it, so the build should check it by region delta-E

dark_fraction.source: photo clusters (the two dark clusters total ~0.36 incl. shading) vs a cited granodiorite dark-mineral share of 12-27 % (search summary)

mineral_colours.status: measured on the photo (apparent colour); not albedo

style.value: BLOCKY / jointed: bounded by near-planar joint and fracture faces meeting at sub-angular edges, with stepped re-entrant notches; surfaces GRANULAR-uneven at grain scale; NOT conchoidal

sources.says: granite is the example of granular fracture
conchoidal fracture is smooth, curved, with concentric ripples; typical of materials without cleavage (glass, flint, quartz)
weathering of jointed bedrock proceeds along intersecting joints, so blocks are joint-bounded
Domokos et al. 2020 (PNAS): natural 3-D fragments average close to a cube; 556 weathered dolomite fragments mean 6.63 faces, 8.93 vertices

style.photo: agrees: about 8-10 distinct planar facets visible, no curved shell-like faces

face_planarity.value: planar at macro scale; deviation from the best-fit plane about 0.5-1 % of face size from granular relief and slight warping (consistent with R2's 1 % bar)
face_planarity.source: R2 constraint (ROUND0.md) + photo shading: each big face shows a near-uniform shade, i.e. a near-constant normal

face_count.source: https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1912.04628 (Domokos et al. 2020; dolomite, a different rock, same fragmentation-geometry claim); notch count from the photo

class.value: sub-angular on the Powers six-class scale (very angular, angular, sub-angular, sub-rounded, rounded, well rounded)

source.says: roundness = mean corner/edge radius over the radius of the largest inscribed sphere; the Powers chart has six classes

radius_mm_at_0.70m.how: by eye on the photo: major ridges (e.g. front block top edge about x 700-900, y 400-450) spread their highlight over about 5-20 px -> 3-13 mm at 0.669 mm/px; larger at the outer corners, smaller on inner notch edges
radius_mm_at_0.70m.status: estimated by eye, NOT tool-measured; the R2 ridge tracer should replace it

roundness_ratio.value: about 0.02-0.05 (edge radius / inscribed radius of about 0.25-0.3 m): edges are only eased, the body stays angular
roundness_ratio.source: derived from the two values above

mechanism.value: weathering attacks corners fastest, edges next, faces slowest, so corners round more than edges

source.says: different weathering rates at corners, edges and faces of a joint block produce rounded cores

definitions.value: axes a >= b >= c (long, intermediate, short) of the smallest bounding box; Zingg classes split at b/a = 2/3 and c/b = 2/3 into equant, oblate (disc), bladed, prolate (rod); C40 = share of clasts with c/a <= 0.4 (slab-like)

sources.says: Zingg factor R = 3/2; four classes equant/prolate/oblate/bladed
axis ratios c/b and b/a are the most established shape descriptors; Zingg's 2/3 cut-off is an arbitrary choice
Bennett et al. 1997: C40 = % of clasts with c/a <= 0.4; supraglacial (rockfall-sourced) clasts are angular

type_prior.value: a joint-bounded blocky granitoid fragment tends to be EQUANT to mildly bladed: b/a 0.65-0.9, c/a 0.45-0.75 (typical b/a 0.75, c/a 0.6)
type_prior.source: estimate, anchored on Domokos et al. 2020 (natural fragments average cube-like: https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1912.04628) and joint-bounded granite blocks (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spheroidal_weathering). NO source found with measured c/a for loose granite boulders (searched rockfall, talus, armourstone; the armourstone standard EN 13383 only limits the share of pieces with length/thickness > 3: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armourstone)

photo_constraint.value: visible width 1047 px (= 0.70 m); height above the contact about 880 px by eye (917 px incl. shadow is an upper bound) under an elevated camera; both left and right flanks recede, so the rock is not a thin slab facing the camera
photo_constraint.confidence: medium for 'not a slab', low for any number

height_over_width.value: take from the photo-fitted camera (R1), not from this pack

min_thickness.value: >= 15 % of the visible depth everywhere (R6); a jointed block has no slivers unless a flake, and none is visible

back_style.value: 3-6 more near-planar facets continuing the visible joint-set orientations (the same 2-3 dominant face-normal families as the front, since joints come in parallel sets), 1-2 stepped notches, same edge radii and grain; NOT a mirror of the front (R6)
back_style.source: joint-set geometry + Domokos mean face count

base.value: a broad, flattish, possibly irregular underside resting on the plane where the contact shadow is darkest; a loose rock comes to rest on a face, not a corner

recommended_for_build.status: ESTIMATED - must be labelled so on the asset (R6; NOTES ruling: the back is estimated and LABELLED)

not_found: A measured c/a or b/a distribution for loose granite/diorite boulders (Domokos 2020 gives axis ratios only as histograms, for dolomite/limestone/gypsum)
Numeric Powers class boundaries from a readable source (Powers 1953 is paywalled: https://archives.datapages.com/data/sepm/journals/v01-32/data/023/023002/0117.htm)
Any way to fix quartz content from a photo: the rock-type call stays medium-low confidence
